text.paragraph: Five-week review: OCD treatment, buprenorphine, pain and the audiogram. [S]

Mr. Hughes returns four weeks after starting buprenorphine and sertraline. Withdrawal settled on the second day of buprenorphine, and on 8 mg twice daily he has no cravings and has taken no other opioid; his bowels are a little slow, and he is drinking more water. He has had four exposure sessions: he now touches door handles and his desk without washing at once, and he lets himself wash for two minutes rather than ten. Washing and checking take about three hours a day. His assistant has attended one session. He has had no side effects from sertraline; no one from the clinic called two weeks after he started it. Physical therapy twice weekly has eased his shoulder. He eats two meals a day. He could not bring himself to use the clinic bathroom today, so no urine test has been done since intake. The audiogram was done this morning. [S]

text.paragraph: Vital signs recorded on 1947-06-08; see the Vital Signs section. [S]

tr.td: Well; blood pressure 118/76, pulse 78; weight 73.4 kg, BMI 20.1
Less tense; no sedation; insight good

Intrusive fears of contamination by germs for about a year, worse since the crash, with hand washing, cleaning of objects and avoidance of handshakes, shared spaces and food handled by others, taking about four hours a day; he recognizes the fears are probably excessive; cause under evaluation
S — Synthetic presenting problem anchored to his documented fear of germs; resolved into the diagnosis of OCD at the consultation. Not a claim about his real symptoms in 1947.
Obsessive-compulsive disorder, contamination type, with good or fair insight, not tic-related; Y-BOCS 28 (severe) at intake; no post-traumatic stress disorder on screening
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis made at the consultation, linked to the retrospective interpretation of his documented fears (R). Not a claim about his real diagnosis.

Opioid use disorder, moderate (four of the DSM-5-TR criteria that count for a prescribed opioid: taking more than prescribed, failed attempts to cut down, time spent getting prescriptions from two prescribers, and craving), on codeine prescribed after a crash; buprenorphine planned
S — Synthetic modern coding; tolerance and withdrawal are not counted for a medicine taken under medical supervision. Person-first language; not a claim about his real diagnosis.
Chronic pain after major trauma ten months ago (crushed chest with rib fractures, collapsed lung, other fractures and burns): chest wall, left shoulder and low back pain, PEG 6.7
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis anchored to his documented injuries.
Difficulty hearing conversation, worse in noise, after years of flying in loud aircraft; cause under evaluation
S — Synthetic presenting problem; resolved into a diagnosis when audiometry was done at five weeks. His documented deafness is from later years.
Bilateral high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss with a notch at 4000 Hz, consistent with noise exposure from flying; hearing aids fitted
S — Synthetic modern diagnosis made at five weeks; not a claim about his real hearing in 1947.
Weight loss of about 8 kg since the crash (BMI 19.7), from eating little outside food he has prepared or inspected himself because of contamination fears
S — Synthetic nutrition problem linked to the contamination fears; not a claim about his real weight in 1947.

list.item:
Obsessive-compulsive disorder (F42.2). Y-BOCS 24, down from 28, after four weeks of sertraline 50 mg and four exposure sessions. Sertraline is well tolerated, so the dose goes up. Safety reviewed: no thoughts of suicide or of harming anyone. [S]
Sertraline 100 mg daily.
Nurse telephone call two weeks after this and every later dose change.
Continue weekly exposure and response prevention.

Opioid use disorder on buprenorphine (F11.20). Stable on 8 mg twice daily with no cravings. The urine test could not be collected because using the clinic bathroom is still beyond his exposure hierarchy. [S]
Continue buprenorphine; dispensed two weeks at a time.
Urine test at the next visit, as a planned exposure with his therapist's help.
More fluids and fiber; a stool softener if needed.

Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss (H90.3). Thresholds 20 dB at 500 Hz, 25 to 30 dB at 1000 Hz, 35 to 40 dB at 1921 Hz and 60 to 65 dB at 4000 Hz in both ears, with a notch at 4000 Hz: noise-induced hearing loss from years of flying loud aircraft. It makes meetings harder and adds to his isolation. [S]
Hearing aids, with a remote microphone for meetings.
Hearing protection when flying and in the factory.

Chronic pain after major trauma (G89.21). PEG 5.7, down from 6.7, on buprenorphine, scheduled acetaminophen and physical therapy. [S]
Continue the current plan.

text.paragraph: Guideline basis: Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (2007); Guideline Watch (March 2013): Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Patients With Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (Koran LM, Simpson HB), as reported by Psychiatric News (2013); Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment (CG31) (2005); CDC Clinical Practice Guideline for Prescribing Opioids for Pain - United States, 2022 (2022); The ASAM National Practice Guideline for the Treatment of Opioid Use Disorder: 2020 Focused Update (2020); Prescription Drug Monitoring Programs (PDMPs) (2026); Hearing loss in adults: assessment and management (NG98) (2018); VA/DoD Clinical Practice Guideline for Assessment and Management of Patients at Risk for Suicide (2024); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monograph (2026)

Follow-up: Nurse telephone call in two weeks. Ten-week review in five weeks, with hearing aid fitting that morning and the urine test as an exposure exercise. Call the clinic or 988 at any time.
